strengths: Addresses a clearly motivated and underexplored problem: caching acceleration specifically tailored to transformer-based Diffusion Policy, as opposed to prior work focused on image/video diffusion U-Net or DiT backbones.
Solid empirical motivation via similarity matrices/curves (Fig. 1, Fig. 10, Fig. 11) showing non-uniform temporal dynamics and block-specific patterns that justify block-wise adaptive scheduling.

The identification of the 'error surge' phenomenon and its theoretical explanation (Proposition 3.1, linearized error-propagation analysis through LayerNorm/FFN) is a nice piece of technical insight that explains why naive block-wise caching fails and motivates the Bubbling Union Algorithm (BUA).
The proposed Adaptive Caching Scheduler (DP-based optimal schedule search) and BUA are simple, training-free, and computationally cheap (computed once per task offline).

Extensive experimental validation: multiple RoboMimic tasks (PH/MH), Push-T, Block Pushing, Kitchen, a VLA model (RDT-1B on ManiSkill), and a real-world Franka arm deployment, plus thorough ablations (choice of similarity metric, hyperparameter n, combination with DDIM) in the appendix.
Good supporting visualizations (cache error heatmaps, feature heatmaps, inter-episode similarity) that substantiate claims about episode homogeneity and cache reliability.
Reports both FLOPs/speedup and practical metrics (inference frequency, end-to-end latency) in real-world tests, showing tangible benefits for real-time control.
weaknesses: Baseline comparison is relatively narrow: only 'Uniform' and an adapted 'TeaCache' are compared; several transformer-diffusion caching methods cited in related work (FORA, δ-DiT, Learning-to-Cache, token-wise caching) are not empirically compared even in adapted form, making it harder to assess relative advantage.

The 'lossless' framing is optimistic given that Table 1/Table 3 show clear performance collapses under certain hyperparameter settings (e.g., BAC(S=5, n=3) average success 0.07, MH Square at S=7 dropping from 0.76 to 0.39), indicating the method is sensitive to the joint choice of S and n and not uniformly robust across tasks.

The method requires per-task offline computation and tuning of at least two hyperparameters (S, n), and their interaction is shown to be non-trivial (Table 3); this adds practical overhead to what is billed as a plug-and-play, training-free method.

Real-world validation is limited to a single manipulation task (bag pick-and-release) on one hardware setup with qualitative rollouts only; no repeated-trial statistics or multiple task variety are reported to support generalizability claims in real deployments.

The limitations section is a single sentence and does not discuss computational/memory overhead of the DP solver at scale, sensitivity to hyperparameters, or applicability to backbones beyond DiT-style Diffusion Policy/VLA.

Reliance on the 'high episode homogeneity' assumption (computed once per task) may not hold in more diverse, open-world, or long-horizon tasks; the evidence provided (Appendix A.15) is restricted to the same benchmarks used for evaluation, so generalization to less homogeneous settings is untested.

Some experimental design choices (e.g., choosing Cosine as default metric, n=5 default) appear to be selected post hoc from the ablation grid rather than justified a priori, raising minor concerns about implicit tuning on the test set of tasks.
